title.narrative: Citizen Science as a tool for Landscape Governance in the SADC region

description.narrative: The overall purpose of the project is to demonstrate the added value of citizen science in governance of landscapes in the SADC region (Southern Africa). The proof of concept will be demonstrated in a number of UNESCO sites, particularly Biosphere Reserves (BR). Since their inception, BR have been promoted as ‘living laboratories’ or ‘learning sites’ that can help scientists, managers, and local communities better understand how to achieve conservation of biodiversity and sustainable development, and are particularly appropriate for promoting integrated monitoring, multidisciplinary approaches, and participatory activities, as well as to develop field learning on sustainability. These “living laboratories” act as sites to test out a variety of solutions, whilst exploring indicators, human perceptions, adaptive capabilities, ecosystem balance and how to replicate and expand to areas outside the BR. Most regional and global policies are promoting sustainable development of communities from the grassroots going upwards. This project seeks to demonstrate that BRs can act as excellent incubators for the use of Citizen Science as a tool for more effective governance. The long‐term Impact the project seeks to achieve is that Citizen science will be used as a pivotal tool for landscape governance in the SADC region, fostering environmental sustainability, community engagement, policy influence, research collaboration, and sustainable development. The rationale for the interventions is that there is a gap and interest in improved local governance in southern Africa, including participation and data for evidence‐based management; and an interest in decolonising research by engaging communities, hence an opportunity to introduce CS as a tool addressing these challenges, but a lack of awareness and experience with CS and proof of concept, which this project seeks to address. To build a sufficient case, within a reasonable timeframe and manageable scope, it has been decided to focus on 3 UNESCO sites who have expressed interest, have strong management capacity, have worked on CS, and have previously collaborated on UNESCO projects with good results. Two of the sites are also part of the SADC TFCA network, since it is a specific target for future replication. Two of the sites are also part of strong RBOs, also a target. In addition, other sites that overlap with the TFCA network will be introduced to the methodologies, in view of generating interest and awareness. The Outcome of the project is therefore Strengthened landscape‐wide governance frameworks and management in minimum 3 UNESCO‐designated sites, through enhanced capacity and participation of stakeholders in citizen science projects. In order to achieve this outcome, a three‐pronged approach will be followed: Component 1 ‐ Enhance capacity and participation in Citizen Science in Biosphere Reserves For 3 focus sites, initially awareness will be raised among the communities and existing and potential new research partners for each site regarding the potential of CS, using resource partners to provide examples and methods used. This includes the WRC‐Citizen Science Association of Southern Africa; and the Vrije Universiteit Brussels’ Citizen Science coordination unit has also been approached to support this output . Their tools will be adapted for southern African context. This output will be followed by facilitation of consultations to develop and agree research plans for each interested research institution with the site, including specific identification of the CS components; and corresponding protocols. It is expected that some of the research institutions will agree to develop comprehensive workplans; while for others the scope will initially be between a department and the site. Subsequently, training for CS teams will be supported. The focus sites are Site 1: Kruger to Canyons Biosphere Reserve (SA) Site 2: Kogelberg Biosphere Reserve (SA) Site 3: Okavango Delta World Heritage Site (Botswana) Component 2 ‐ Strengthen landscape management in Biosphere Reserves The second component of the project will make the link between discrete CS actions and governance of each of the focus sites. Evidence‐based management requires a monitoring system with relevant indicators. Firstly, the current scope and status of monitoring in the landscape will be assessed, and a gaps/needs analysis conducted, to lead to an agreed indicator framework. In addition to the agreed CS actions with scientific institutions, the project will support additional monitoring capacity in function of the agreed framework. This will include building on existing resources that UNESCO has developed in the Be Resilient programme, such as the Citizen Science Smartphone Data Collection Tool and Data Visualisation Platform. Component 3 ‐ Strengthen landscape Governance Frameworks and Policies in Southern Africa The third set of outputs seeks to advocate for wider awareness of the achievements in the first 2 components and replication. Key stakeholders are national and regional MAB and IHP Committees, and SADC TFCA partners (the SADC secretariat and the implementing partners, particularly GIZ and IUCN). These will be briefed and engaged during the inception phase. The collaboration with SADC in TFCAs and with RBOs is already integrated in the Joint Plan of Action; and partners have expressed interest in the CS approach.
